# Kirn Docs — full content bundle

# AI-readable documentation

Source: https://rkriad585.github.io/kirn/guide/ai

Use the Kirn documentation as a compact, structured context source.

# AI-readable documentation

Kirn Docs publishes machine-readable context alongside the human documentation:

- [`llms.txt`](/kirn/llms.txt) — a compact index of the documentation and ecosystem links.
- [`llms-full.txt`](/kirn/llms-full.txt) — a single Markdown bundle containing the full page text.
- [`ai/docs.json`](/kirn/ai/docs.json) — structured page metadata, canonical URLs, and stable source paths.

These files are generated from the same Markdown pages used by VitePress. They are useful for coding assistants, search indexes, offline readers, and retrieval pipelines.

## Recommended retrieval flow

1. Fetch `llms.txt` to discover available pages.
2. Fetch individual page URLs when focused context is needed.
3. Use `ai/docs.json` for metadata or a complete page inventory.
4. Use `llms-full.txt` when one context bundle is more useful than multiple requests.

The source repository is [github.com/rkriad585/kirn](https://github.com/rkriad585/kirn). Documentation examples should be checked against the current compiler before being treated as implementation guarantees.

---

# CLI workflow

Source: https://rkriad585.github.io/kirn/guide/cli

Use the Kirn command-line driver to run, test, build, and manage projects.

# CLI workflow

The `kirn` driver is the main entry point.

| Command | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `kirn run file.kn` | Run a program |
| `kirn new name` | Scaffold a project |
| `kirn test` | Run tests |
| `kirn build` | Build a program |
| `kirn install` | Install a package |
| `kirn add` | Add a dependency |
| `kirn update` | Update dependencies |
| `kirn remove` | Remove a dependency |
| `kirn doc` | Serve Markdown and API documentation |

## A normal loop

```bash
kirn new hello
cd hello
kirn run code/main.kn
kirn test
kirn build --release
```

Build options include `--debug`, `--release`, `--target`, `--native`, `--asan`, `-S`, `-O`, and `-o`. Run `kirn` without arguments for the current help output.

---

# Contributing

Source: https://rkriad585.github.io/kirn/guide/contributing

Help improve Kirn and its documentation.

# Contributing

Kirn is built in public. The best contributions are focused, reproducible, and honest about what the compiler currently supports.

## Code contributions

1. Read the repository's [contributing guide](https://github.com/rkriad585/kirn/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md).
2. Build the project and run the relevant example or test.
3. Keep a change focused and explain the behavior it verifies.
4. Open a pull request with reproduction and verification notes.

## Documentation contributions

Documentation examples should run with the current toolchain. If a claim compares Kirn with another language or promises a future feature, include a source or benchmark and label roadmap work clearly.

The docs site lives in `docs-site/` and is deployed by GitHub Actions. Run `npm install` and `npm run docs:build` there before opening a docs pull request.

---

# Project structure

Source: https://rkriad585.github.io/kirn/guide/project

Understand a Kirn project scaffold and kirn.toml.

# Project structure

`kirn new demo` creates a project with a manifest, source tree, tests, and documentation:

```text
demo/
├── kirn.toml
├── code/
│   └── main.kn
├── tests/
├── docs/
└── .gitignore
```

The manifest describes package metadata and dependencies:

```toml
[package]
name = "demo"
version = "0.1.0"
type = "bin"
main = "code/main.kn"
license = "MIT"

[dependencies]
```

Keep examples and tests close to the project. A package is easier to understand when its source, docs, and executable checks evolve together.

---

# Build targets

Source: https://rkriad585.github.io/kirn/guide/toolchain

Understand Kirn bytecode, native builds, and supported target shapes.

# Build targets

Kirn's toolchain can run source directly, produce bytecode bundles, and build native artifacts. The exact backend and target support are under active development.

```bash
kirn build --debug
kirn build --release
kirn build --native
kirn targets
```

The project tracks platform families across Windows, Linux, and Darwin, with amd64 and arm64 target shapes. Treat a target as supported only when the current CI or release workflow proves it.

## Output forms

- `.bkn` — bytecode bundle.
- `.kirnlib` — library package.
- Native executable output — platform-specific executable.

For compiler architecture, read the source pipeline from lexer and parser through semantic analysis, VM, interpreter, and native backend.

## Toolchain at a glance

~~~mermaid
flowchart LR
  Source[".kn source"] --> Lexer["Lexer"]
  Lexer --> Parser["Parser"]
  Parser --> Check["Semantic checks"]
  Check --> Run["Interpreter / VM"]
  Check --> Native["Native backend"]
  Run --> Output["Program output"]
  Native --> Output
~~~

The same pipeline is available as a readable [toolchain guide](/guide/toolchain) and in the source repository.

# Functions and control flow

Source: https://rkriad585.github.io/kirn/learn/basics/functions

Define functions and compose expressions in Kirn.

# Functions and control flow

Functions use `fn`, a name, parameters, and a body. A final expression can be returned from a block.

```kirn
fn classify(value: Int) -> Str {
    if value < 0 {
        "negative"
    } elif value == 0 {
        "zero"
    } else {
        "positive"
    }
}
```

Kirn includes `if`, `elif`, and `else`, plus `while` and `for` loops. Ranges use `..` and `..=` forms.

```kirn
for number in 1..=5 {
    print(number);
}
```

Closures can capture values from the surrounding scope. See the verified examples in `examples/06_functions_params.kn` and `examples/07_closures_captures.kn`.

---

# Variables and values

Source: https://rkriad585.github.io/kirn/learn/basics/variables

Bind values and use type annotations in Kirn.

# Variables and values

Kirn supports inferred values and explicit type annotations. Bindings are immutable by default; use the language's mutable-binding forms only when the program needs them.

```kirn
count: Int = 3;
ratio: Float = 0.5;
label: Str = "ready";
enabled: Bool = true;
```

Literal values include numbers, strings, booleans, characters, lists, dictionaries, and sets. The canonical primitive names are capitalized:

```kirn
age = 25;
title = "A small program";
scores = [10, 20, 30];
```

Use the [Types reference](/reference/language/types) for the current primitive and container families.

---

# Concurrency

Source: https://rkriad585.github.io/kirn/learn/beyond/concurrency

Explore Kirn's spawn, channel, select, and join primitives.

# Concurrency

Kirn includes language-level building blocks for concurrent programs. The verified example corpus covers green-thread-style `spawn`, channels, `select`, and `join`.

```kirn
channel = chan<Int>();

spawn {
    channel <- 42;
}

value = <-channel;
print(value);
```

Concurrency behavior and runtime guarantees are still developing. Start with `examples/22_spawn_channels_join.kn` and `examples/23_select_multiplex.kn`, then test changes against the current toolchain.

---

# Optionals and results

Source: https://rkriad585.github.io/kirn/learn/data/optionals-results

Represent missing values and recoverable errors in Kirn.

# Optionals and results

Optional types use `?` to express that a value may be absent:

```kirn
fn find_name(id: Int) -> Str? {
    if id == 1 { "Ada" } else { none }
}
```

The nil-safe access operator `.?.` helps inspect an optional value without pretending it is always present.

Results model success and failure explicitly. The `try` form propagates a failure to the caller:

```kirn
fn load_config(path: Str) -> Result<Config, Error> {
    text = try read_file(path);
    parse_config(text)
}
```

The exact result and optional APIs are evolving; use the compiler and standard-library reference as the current authority.

---

# Structs and enums

Source: https://rkriad585.github.io/kirn/learn/data/structs-enums

Model structured data with structs and enums.

# Structs and enums

Use a `struct` to group named fields and behavior:

```kirn
struct User {
    name: Str;
    active: Bool;
}

fn main() {
    user = User(name: "Riad", active: true);
    print(user.name);
}
```

Enums represent a closed set of variants and work naturally with `match`:

```kirn
enum Status {
    Ready,
    Done,
}

fn label(status: Status) -> Str {
    match status {
        case Status.Ready => "ready";
        case Status.Done => "done";
    }
}
```

See [syntax and operators](/reference/language/syntax) for pattern details.

---

# Installation

Source: https://rkriad585.github.io/kirn/learn/installation

Build and run the Kirn toolchain from source.

# Installation

Kirn is currently developed from source. The repository is the authoritative place for supported build instructions and platform changes.

## Get the source

```bash
git clone https://github.com/rkriad585/kirn.git
cd kirn
```

Kirn uses CMake and a C++20 toolchain. Build instructions may vary by platform; check the repository README and CI workflow for the current dependency list.

## Verify the checkout

After building, confirm that the driver is available:

```bash
kirn
kirn run examples/01_hello.kn
```

The example corpus is intentionally useful: it gives you small programs to run while learning the language and a concrete way to check whether a feature is implemented.

## Next step

Continue with the [Quick start](/learn/quick-start), or read the [CLI guide](/guide/cli) for the full workflow.

# Introduction

Source: https://rkriad585.github.io/kirn/learn/introduction

What Kirn is, who it is for, and how to read the documentation.

# Introduction

Kirn is a general-purpose programming language created by [RK Riad Khan](https://rkriad585.github.io/). Its design aims to keep readable source, explicit structure, and a compiled toolchain close together.

The language is open source and actively evolving. The most useful way to understand it is to run the examples in the [official repository](https://github.com/rkriad585/kirn), then use these docs as a map.

## What Kirn gives you

- Familiar, expression-oriented syntax for small programs and larger systems.
- Strong types, structs, enums, traits, generics, and optionals.
- Functions, closures, modules, pattern matching, and error propagation.
- Concurrency primitives including `spawn`, channels, `select`, and `join`.
- A CLI for running, testing, building, packaging, and documenting projects.

Kirn is not finished. Claims about performance, ownership, networking, IDE support, or future tooling should be treated as roadmap material unless they are backed by the source and a runnable example.

## Choose your path

- **New to Kirn?** Continue to [Installation](/learn/installation), then [Quick start](/learn/quick-start).
- **Know the basics?** Read the [CLI workflow](/guide/cli) and [Project structure](/guide/project).
- **Looking for exact syntax?** Open the [Language reference](/reference/language/lexical).
- **Looking for packages?** Visit the [Pets registry](https://pets-registry.github.io/).

## Source of truth

The normative grammar lives in `grammar/kirn.ebnf`. The canonical keyword set is maintained by the lexer. Examples in `examples/` are the working corpus used to validate language behavior.

---

# Quick start

Source: https://rkriad585.github.io/kirn/learn/quick-start

Write and run your first Kirn program.

# Quick start

Create a file named `hello.kn`:

```kirn
fn main() {
    name = "Kirn";
    print(f"Hello, {name}!");
}
```

Run it with the Kirn driver:

```bash
kirn run hello.kn
```

## A small function

Kirn programs can describe a value with a function and return it to the caller:

```kirn
fn greet(name: Str) -> Str {
    f"Hello, {name}!"
}

fn main() {
    message = greet("builder");
    print(message);
}
```

The exact set of built-ins and accepted syntax follows the compiler in the source repository. When an example differs from the current compiler, trust a runnable example and report the mismatch.

## Where to go next

- [Variables and values](/learn/basics/variables)
- [Functions and control flow](/learn/basics/functions)
- [Project structure](/guide/project)

# Lexical structure

Source: https://rkriad585.github.io/kirn/reference/language/lexical

Learn Kirn identifiers, comments, keywords, and literals.

# Lexical structure

Kirn source files use the `.kn` extension. Whitespace is not significant; blocks use braces and simple statements normally end with semicolons.

## Identifiers

Identifiers begin with a letter or underscore and may contain numbers after the first character.

```kirn
user_name = "kirn";
_count = 1;
```

## Comments

A comment begins with `#` and continues to the end of the line.

```kirn
# This is a comment.
value = 42;
```

## Keywords

The lexer currently recognizes keywords including `fn`, `var`, `if`, `elif`, `else`, `while`, `for`, `in`, `return`, `match`, `struct`, `enum`, `trait`, `impl`, `import`, `export`, `pub`, `spawn`, `chan`, `select`, `try`, `catch`, `unsafe`, `extern`, `class`, `interface`, `record`, and `extends`.

The authoritative list is `src/lex/lexer.cpp`; syntax is specified in `grammar/kirn.ebnf`.

---

# Syntax and operators

Source: https://rkriad585.github.io/kirn/reference/language/syntax

Explore Kirn expressions, statements, patterns, and operators.

# Syntax and operators

Kirn uses braces for blocks and semicolons for simple statements. Expressions can appear where a value is expected, including conditional and match expressions.

## Operators

The grammar includes arithmetic, comparison, boolean, range, assignment, bitwise, and propagation operators.

```text
+  -  *  /  %       ==  !=  <  <=  >  >=
and  or  not        ..  ..=      ?.  .?.
->  <-              +=  -=  *=  /=  %= 
```

Operator precedence is defined by `grammar/kirn.ebnf`. When in doubt, use parentheses and consult the grammar rather than relying on a language from memory.

## Pattern matching

```kirn
match value {
    case 0 => "zero";
    case n if n > 0 => "positive";
    case _ => "negative";
}
```

Patterns, guards, destructuring, and ranges are covered by the example corpus.

---

# Types

Source: https://rkriad585.github.io/kirn/reference/language/types

Reference Kirn primitive, container, optional, and result types.

# Types

Canonical primitive names are capitalized: `Int`, `UInt`, `Float`, `UFloat`, `Bool`, `Str`, `Char`, `BigInt`, and `Rational`.

Width families include forms such as `Int32`, `UInt64`, `Float32`, `i32`, `u64`, and `f64`. The grammar also includes `usize`, `isize`, character widths, and byte forms.

## Compound types

Kirn supports type forms for lists, dictionaries, sets, functions, optionals, and results:

```kirn
names: list<Str>;
lookup: dict<Str, Int>;
maybe: Int?;
work: fn(Int) -> Str;
```

Type syntax and accepted aliases can change before the grammar is frozen. The EBNF and checker are the source of truth.

---

# collections

Source: https://rkriad585.github.io/kirn/reference/stdlib/collections

Collection helpers in the Kirn standard library.

# `collections`

The collections module covers common operations on lists, sets, and related values. Source-backed helpers include `unique`, `shuffle`, and `rand_float`.

Use the collection examples and tests to understand mutation, value semantics, and iteration behavior.

---

# core

Source: https://rkriad585.github.io/kirn/reference/stdlib/core

Core values and built-in operations in Kirn.

# `core`

Core functionality is available to every Kirn program. It includes primitive values, conversions, comparisons, and the built-in operations used by language examples.

Use the current source and tests as the API authority. The core surface is intentionally small so programs can build on predictable language primitives.

---

# Standard library

Source: https://rkriad585.github.io/kirn/reference/stdlib

Overview of the Kirn standard library modules.

# Standard library

The standard library is organized into small modules. The current source tree includes `core`, `io`, `math`, `strings`, `collections`, `json`, `os`, `path`, `regexp`, `time`, and `text/slug`.

Each module is backed by source and test files in the repository. Use the pages in this section as a map, then inspect the module and its tests for the exact current signatures.

- [core](/reference/stdlib/core)
- [io](/reference/stdlib/io)
- [math](/reference/stdlib/math)
- [strings](/reference/stdlib/strings)
- [collections](/reference/stdlib/collections)
- [json](/reference/stdlib/json)
- [os and path](/reference/stdlib/os-path)
- [regexp and time](/reference/stdlib/regexp-time)

---

# io

Source: https://rkriad585.github.io/kirn/reference/stdlib/io

Input and output helpers in the Kirn standard library.

# `io`

The `io` module provides file and stream operations used by programs that interact with the local environment.

Common source-backed operations include reading and writing files. Check the module tests for accepted arguments, error behavior, and platform details.

```kirn
text = read_file("notes.txt");
write_file("copy.txt", text);
```

---

# json

Source: https://rkriad585.github.io/kirn/reference/stdlib/json

Encode and decode JSON values in Kirn.

# `json`

The JSON module provides `dumps` and `loads` for converting between Kirn values and JSON text.

```kirn
payload = {"name": "Kirn", "active": true};
text = dumps(payload);
value = loads(text);
```

Use the source and tests for supported value shapes and error cases.

---

# math

Source: https://rkriad585.github.io/kirn/reference/stdlib/math

Mathematical helpers in the Kirn standard library.

# `math`

The math module includes source-backed helpers such as `sqrt`, `abs`, `clamp`, `min2`, `max2`, `ipow`, and `fpow`.

```kirn
root = sqrt(16.0);
safe = clamp(root, 0.0, 3.0);
```

Check the module tests for numeric types and edge cases.

---

# os and path

Source: https://rkriad585.github.io/kirn/reference/stdlib/os-path

Work with process arguments, environment, and filesystem paths.

# `os` and `path`

The `os` module exposes process-oriented helpers such as arguments, environment lookup, and exit behavior. The `path` module provides path operations.

```kirn
args = args();
home = getenv("HOME");
```

Platform-specific behavior should be verified on the target you intend to ship.

---

# regexp and time

Source: https://rkriad585.github.io/kirn/reference/stdlib/regexp-time

Pattern matching and time helpers in the Kirn standard library.

# `regexp` and `time`

These modules provide regular-expression and time-related building blocks. Their APIs are evolving with the standard library, so use the module source and tests as the final reference.

The docs site will expand these pages as stable public signatures and verified examples are established.

---

# strings

Source: https://rkriad585.github.io/kirn/reference/stdlib/strings

String operations in the Kirn standard library.

# `strings`

String helpers include searching, replacing, splitting, joining, repetition, reversing, padding, and stripping.

```kirn
clean = strip("  kirn  ");
parts = split(clean, " ");
joined = join(parts, "-");
```

The exact signatures are maintained in the source-backed module and its tests.
